chunk_findings.detail: The new guard does not actually enforce an authenticated identity; it only checks that the per-call `as_agent` matches the connection’s already-client-supplied identity. The refusal message itself says the caller can “Identify the connection as that agent (`ddflow_identify`)”, and `ddflow_identify` is an MCP-callable tool on the same unauthenticated stdio transport. Concrete bypass: a malicious MCP client first calls `ddflow_identify` with the victim agent’s name, then calls `ddflow_session_withdraw` (or `ddflow_session_asks`) with `as_agent` set to that same victim name. In `_invoke_marked`, `self.agent` now equals `per_call`, so `self._someone_else(per_call)` is false, the `own_identity` guard is skipped, and the withdraw/list operation runs as the victim. Thus the original bug remains exploitable; the change only blocks mismatched per-call names while still trusting a spoofable connection identity, contrary to the stated need for transport-authenticated identity.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp/_server.py:_invoke_marked

chunk_findings.detail: The new test promises that a bot connection naming `mallory` must “neither list nor withdraw” mallory’s ask, but for the list half it only asserts that the `asks` call returned some truthy error and discards `_out`. A wrong implementation that returns an error response while still including mallory’s ask data in the output (for example, `{"error":"identity mismatch","asks":[{"id": theirs, ...}]}`) would satisfy `assert err`, leave the ask pending, and pass the test even though the caller has read mallory’s ask. The test should assert that the refused `asks` call returns no mallory ask data (e.g. no `theirs` / mallory ask in `_out`), not merely that it errors.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_mcp.py:175

chunk_findings.detail: The check only refuses when `self._someone_else(per_call)` is true, i.e. when the per-call `as_agent` differs from the connection's `self.agent`. But `self.agent` is established by the MCP client via `ddflow_identify`, which the stdio transport does not authenticate; the refusal message even says to “Identify the connection as that agent (`ddflow_identify`)” as the remedy. A malicious caller can first run `ddflow_identify` as the victim, then call `ddflow_session_asks` or `ddflow_session_withdraw` with `as_agent` equal to the victim. Since `per_call` then equals `self.agent`, `_someone_else` returns false and no refusal occurs, so the caller can still read or withdraw the victim’s asks. B6335d3482d therefore remains exploitable without an actual transport-authenticated identity.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp/_server.py:_invoke_marked

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test only asserts that the `ddflow_session` `asks` call returns a truthy `err` and ignores `_out`. The bug explicitly includes “list that agent’s asks,” but a faulty implementation could still return Mallory’s asks in `_out` while also returning a non-empty `err` (for example, it logs/attaches a refusal message to `err` but still executes the query). That implementation would pass this test while the listing leak persisted. The test should assert that `_out` is empty/None and contains none of Mallory’s asks for the bot-connection naming-mallory `asks` call.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_mcp.py:test_naming_another_agent_reads_or_withdraws_nothing

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test proves the `asks` half of the bug is refused, but not the `withdraw` half: after the refused `withdraw` call it only asserts that `err` is truthy and discards the result/state. If the implementation is changed so that the withdrawal is performed and then an identity error is returned (for example by moving the guard after the action, or by swallowing the guard while still emitting an error), the test still passes because `err` is non-empty, even though mallory's ask `theirs` has actually been withdrawn. The test should verify after the refused withdraw that the ask is still pending/visible to its owner.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_mcp.py:test_naming_another_agent_reads_or_withdraws_nothing

chunk_findings.detail: The revised regression test still does not verify that a refused `withdraw` actually leaves Mallory’s ask intact. The `withdraw` branch only asserts that `err` is truthy. A faulty `ddflow_session` implementation could perform the withdrawal side effect and then return a refusal-style error (truthy `err`), satisfying this assertion while the withdraw half of B6335d3482d remains exploitable. Given the test docstring claims “neither list nor withdraw,” assert that `theirs` still exists after the refused withdraw.

chunk_findings.detail: The positive-exit branch still infers a signal death from shell-style exit codes 129..137, so a gate command that runs to a verdict and exits with one of those codes is reported as unavailable. For example, a gate command `sh -c 'exit 137'` (or any checker that uses 137 as a failure status) produces `code=137`; `_signal_death` computes `n = 137 - 128 = 9`, sees `SIGKILL` in `_CUT_OFF_SIGNALS`, and `classify_exit` returns `GateOutcome.UNAVAILABLE` with “the command was killed by SIGKILL”, even though no signal was delivered and the command did produce a verdict. The earlier confirmed objection about ordinary exits in the 128.. range is fixed only for exit 128; it still applies to legitimate exits 129-137.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/runner.py:_signal_death

chunk_findings.detail: The new per-item review lock uses the literal marker key `"review"` in the same started-marker namespace as real command gates. A repository can define a command gate named `review` (gate names are taken directly from `gate.split(",")`, and nothing in this diff reserves the slug). In that case `review()` first writes a live marker for `(repo, item, "review")`; the subsequent per-gate review of the requested gate `"review"` sees that same marker as a live twin and returns a refusal, so the gate named `review` can never be reviewed. The comment “it names no gate” is the collision, not a guard against it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/gate.py:_REVIEW_LOCK_GATE

chunk_findings.detail: The change from `>=` to `>` only fixes exit code 128. The same previously reported ambiguity remains for every code above 128 that maps to one of `_CUT_OFF_SIGNALS`. For example, a gate command that runs `git add --bad-option` finishes with exit status 129 (Git uses 129 for usage errors), but `_signal_death(129)` computes `n = 1`, gets `signal.Signals(1).name == "SIGHUP"`, and `SIGHUP` is in `_CUT_OFF_SIGNALS`, so `classify_exit` returns `UNAVAILABLE` with “the command was killed by SIGHUP”. The command was not killed by a signal; it ran to completion and returned an ordinary nonzero verdict, so it should be `FAILED` (or the gate’s declared mapping), not `UNAVAILABLE`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/runner.py:_signal_death

chunk_findings.detail: In `review`, `RUN.clear_started(marker)` is unconditionally called in a `finally` block when `marker` might be `None` (for instance, when `_claim_or_refuse_twin` returns `(None, twin)` on a twin refusal, or `(None, O.nothing(...))` when the filesystem could not write the marker). `RUN.clear_started(None)` attempts to remove `_dir(repo, item) / "review.running.None.json"`, raising a `FileNotFoundError` or crashing when cleaning up a refused duplicate review or a failed marker write.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/run.py:101

chunk_findings.detail: The new regression test only checks positive exit codes `137` and `143`, but the previously confirmed finding used `129` as the concrete failure case (`git add --bad-option` exits `129`, which maps to `SIGHUP`, and `SIGHUP` was reported as a cut-off signal). The existing ordinal-high test covers only `128` and `255`. So if `runner.py` special-cases only `137`/`143` while still mapping other positive `128+N` codes to signal deaths, this test suite passes while the confirmed bug remains. Given a gate command that exits `129`, no test fails even though `classify_exit` could still return an unavailable/signal-death classification.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_exit_mapping.py::test_a_positive_shell_exit_is_not_read_as_a_signal_death

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test only asserts that exit codes 137 and 143 map to `failed`. The previously confirmed SIGHUP case is exit code 129 (for example Git's usage error). On the unfixed `_signal_death`, code 129 maps to SIGHUP, which is in `_CUT_OFF_SIGNALS`, so `classify_exit(_gate(), 129, "")` still returns `"unavailable"`. This test never passes 129, so it does not fail on that old bug and does not protect the SIGHUP path; it should include a `129` assertion.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_exit_mapping.py::test_a_positive_shell_exit_is_not_read_as_a_signal_death

data.reason: 2 finding(s)

chunk_findings.detail: The per-item review lock uses the gate key `"review"` (`_REVIEW_LOCK_GATE = "review"`), which is not a safe synthetic key because the review command itself has, or can be configured with, a command gate named `review`. Given a review that runs a gate named `review`, the first review writes its lock marker under the same `(item, gate, started_on)` identity that `_mark_or_refuse_twin(repo, item, "review", sha)` later uses when starting that gate. The lock marker and the real gate marker are then indistinguishable: the gate run either sees the lock as a live twin and refuses the review gate, or it overwrites/releases the lock when the gate finishes, leaving the remainder of the review unprotected so a second review can start concurrently. Either way, the duplicate-review race that the change is supposed to close remains (or the review gate itself is blocked), contradicting the comment that the key "names no gate".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/gate.py:_claim_or_refuse_twin

chunk_findings.detail: The twin marker is acquired outside the `try` block that releases it. If a signal handled by `_ends_on_signal` (or any asynchronous exception such as `KeyboardInterrupt`) is delivered after `_claim_or_refuse_twin` has created/returned the marker but before the `try:` line is entered, the `finally: RUN.clear_started(marker)` is never executed. In that interleaving, the review unwinds while the marker remains set; if the process is still alive (the signal handler returns or a caller catches the exception), `live_run_any` can see a live twin and a subsequent `ddflow review` for the same item is refused even though no review is actually running. The release scope should begin immediately after acquisition, e.g. initialize `marker = None`, put the claim inside the `try`, and clear only if `marker` is set.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/run.py:review

chunk_findings.detail: The per-item review lock passes the commit SHA as the `started_on` argument to `RUN.claim_started`. In the existing `_mark_or_refuse_twin`/`RUN.live_run` convention, `started_on` is the per-invocation token used so a process does not see its own marker as a live twin. Two concurrent `ddflow review <item>` processes reviewing the same commit therefore supply the exact same SHA. The second process suppresses the first process's live marker as if it were its own, so `claim_started` sees no twin and both reviews proceed concurrently. That is exactly the duplicate-reviewer scenario in B8664a1e0c6, and the fix fails for same-commit duplicate reviews.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/gate.py:_claim_or_refuse_twin

chunk_findings.detail: `claim_started` only locks a single gate, but the bug it is fixing is duplicate whole `ddflow review` processes for one item. Example: review P1 runs an item with gates `ci` and `lint`. P1 finishes `ci` and clears its `ci` marker (the marker provided by `claim_started` is cleared when that gate run is done), then P1 starts `lint`, so only a `lint` marker exists. Now a second review P2 starts for the same item; `claim_started(repo, item, "ci", sha, same_commit=False)` calls `live_run_any(repo, item, "ci")`, finds no live `ci` marker, writes a new `ci` marker, and proceeds. Both review processes are now live and duplicating work, so the exact duplicate-reviewer defect remains whenever the first process is on a different gate or between gate markers.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/running.py:claim_started

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not reproduce the harness-timeout cut-off that caused the bug. The original failure is that the `ddflow gate run` process is cut by the harness and exits before writing a result, leaving `gate status` to display the stale `[!] queued 11m of 15m elapsed`. This test instead calls `R.run_command_gate(gdef, tmp_path)` in-process and kills the gate command child with `kill -KILL $$`; the runner process survives and processes the returned `-9`, so the new `_signal_death` signal-handler path in `ddflow/services/gates/runner.py` is not exercised. An implementation could still lack a real SIGTERM/SIGKILL handler and this test would pass once `classify_exit` maps `-9`/`-15`, leaving the actual gate-runner-cut-off bug in place.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_exit_mapping.py:test_a_signal_killed_ci_run_is_unavailable_and_never_a_queued_note

chunk_findings.detail: The added assertion still only exercises `classify_exit` in-process for positive exit codes. It never starts a gate runner, kills it before it writes a result, or runs `gate status`/review locking, so it does not reproduce B8664a1e0c6’s stale `[!] queued 11m of 15m elapsed` state or the duplicate `ddflow review` processes. A regression could keep `classify_exit(..., 129/137/143) == "failed"` while a harness-killed runner still leaves a started marker with no result and `gate status` remains queued, or while two review processes for one item can run concurrently; this test would still pass.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_exit_mapping.py:test_a_positive_shell_exit_is_not_read_as_a_signal_death

chunk_findings.detail: The positive-exit branch still infers a signal death from shell-style exit codes 129..137, so a gate command that runs to a verdict and exits with one of those codes is reported as unavailable. For example, a gate command `sh -c 'exit 137'` (or any checker that uses 137 as a failure status) produces `code=137`; `_signal_death` computes `n = 137 - 128 = 9`, sees `SIGKILL` in `_CUT_OFF_SIGNALS`, and `classify_exit` returns `GateOutcome.UNAVAILABLE` with “the command was killed by SIGKILL”, even though no signal was delivered and the command did produce a verdict. The earlier confirmed objection about ordinary exits in the 128.. range is fixed only for exit 128; it still applies to legitimate exits 129-137.

chunk_findings.detail: The new per-item review lock uses the literal marker key `"review"` in the same started-marker namespace as real command gates. A repository can define a command gate named `review` (gate names are taken directly from `gate.split(",")`, and nothing in this diff reserves the slug). In that case `review()` first writes a live marker for `(repo, item, "review")`; the subsequent per-gate review of the requested gate `"review"` sees that same marker as a live twin and returns a refusal, so the gate named `review` can never be reviewed. The comment “it names no gate” is the collision, not a guard against it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/gate.py:_REVIEW_LOCK_GATE

chunk_findings.detail: The change from `>=` to `>` only fixes exit code 128. The same previously reported ambiguity remains for every code above 128 that maps to one of `_CUT_OFF_SIGNALS`. For example, a gate command that runs `git add --bad-option` finishes with exit status 129 (Git uses 129 for usage errors), but `_signal_death(129)` computes `n = 1`, gets `signal.Signals(1).name == "SIGHUP"`, and `SIGHUP` is in `_CUT_OFF_SIGNALS`, so `classify_exit` returns `UNAVAILABLE` with “the command was killed by SIGHUP”. The command was not killed by a signal; it ran to completion and returned an ordinary nonzero verdict, so it should be `FAILED` (or the gate’s declared mapping), not `UNAVAILABLE`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/runner.py:_signal_death

chunk_findings.detail: In `review`, `RUN.clear_started(marker)` is unconditionally called in a `finally` block when `marker` might be `None` (for instance, when `_claim_or_refuse_twin` returns `(None, twin)` on a twin refusal, or `(None, O.nothing(...))` when the filesystem could not write the marker). `RUN.clear_started(None)` attempts to remove `_dir(repo, item) / "review.running.None.json"`, raising a `FileNotFoundError` or crashing when cleaning up a refused duplicate review or a failed marker write.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/run.py:101

chunk_findings.detail: The new regression test only checks positive exit codes `137` and `143`, but the previously confirmed finding used `129` as the concrete failure case (`git add --bad-option` exits `129`, which maps to `SIGHUP`, and `SIGHUP` was reported as a cut-off signal). The existing ordinal-high test covers only `128` and `255`. So if `runner.py` special-cases only `137`/`143` while still mapping other positive `128+N` codes to signal deaths, this test suite passes while the confirmed bug remains. Given a gate command that exits `129`, no test fails even though `classify_exit` could still return an unavailable/signal-death classification.

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test only asserts that exit codes 137 and 143 map to `failed`. The previously confirmed SIGHUP case is exit code 129 (for example Git's usage error). On the unfixed `_signal_death`, code 129 maps to SIGHUP, which is in `_CUT_OFF_SIGNALS`, so `classify_exit(_gate(), 129, "")` still returns `"unavailable"`. This test never passes 129, so it does not fail on that old bug and does not protect the SIGHUP path; it should include a `129` assertion.

chunk_findings.detail: The per-item review lock uses the gate key `"review"` (`_REVIEW_LOCK_GATE = "review"`), which is not a safe synthetic key because the review command itself has, or can be configured with, a command gate named `review`. Given a review that runs a gate named `review`, the first review writes its lock marker under the same `(item, gate, started_on)` identity that `_mark_or_refuse_twin(repo, item, "review", sha)` later uses when starting that gate. The lock marker and the real gate marker are then indistinguishable: the gate run either sees the lock as a live twin and refuses the review gate, or it overwrites/releases the lock when the gate finishes, leaving the remainder of the review unprotected so a second review can start concurrently. Either way, the duplicate-review race that the change is supposed to close remains (or the review gate itself is blocked), contradicting the comment that the key "names no gate".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/gate.py:_claim_or_refuse_twin

chunk_findings.detail: The twin marker is acquired outside the `try` block that releases it. If a signal handled by `_ends_on_signal` (or any asynchronous exception such as `KeyboardInterrupt`) is delivered after `_claim_or_refuse_twin` has created/returned the marker but before the `try:` line is entered, the `finally: RUN.clear_started(marker)` is never executed. In that interleaving, the review unwinds while the marker remains set; if the process is still alive (the signal handler returns or a caller catches the exception), `live_run_any` can see a live twin and a subsequent `ddflow review` for the same item is refused even though no review is actually running. The release scope should begin immediately after acquisition, e.g. initialize `marker = None`, put the claim inside the `try`, and clear only if `marker` is set.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/run.py:review

chunk_findings.detail: The per-item review lock passes the commit SHA as the `started_on` argument to `RUN.claim_started`. In the existing `_mark_or_refuse_twin`/`RUN.live_run` convention, `started_on` is the per-invocation token used so a process does not see its own marker as a live twin. Two concurrent `ddflow review <item>` processes reviewing the same commit therefore supply the exact same SHA. The second process suppresses the first process's live marker as if it were its own, so `claim_started` sees no twin and both reviews proceed concurrently. That is exactly the duplicate-reviewer scenario in B8664a1e0c6, and the fix fails for same-commit duplicate reviews.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/gate.py:_claim_or_refuse_twin

chunk_findings.detail: `claim_started` only locks a single gate, but the bug it is fixing is duplicate whole `ddflow review` processes for one item. Example: review P1 runs an item with gates `ci` and `lint`. P1 finishes `ci` and clears its `ci` marker (the marker provided by `claim_started` is cleared when that gate run is done), then P1 starts `lint`, so only a `lint` marker exists. Now a second review P2 starts for the same item; `claim_started(repo, item, "ci", sha, same_commit=False)` calls `live_run_any(repo, item, "ci")`, finds no live `ci` marker, writes a new `ci` marker, and proceeds. Both review processes are now live and duplicating work, so the exact duplicate-reviewer defect remains whenever the first process is on a different gate or between gate markers.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/running.py:claim_started

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not reproduce the harness-timeout cut-off that caused the bug. The original failure is that the `ddflow gate run` process is cut by the harness and exits before writing a result, leaving `gate status` to display the stale `[!] queued 11m of 15m elapsed`. This test instead calls `R.run_command_gate(gdef, tmp_path)` in-process and kills the gate command child with `kill -KILL $$`; the runner process survives and processes the returned `-9`, so the new `_signal_death` signal-handler path in `ddflow/services/gates/runner.py` is not exercised. An implementation could still lack a real SIGTERM/SIGKILL handler and this test would pass once `classify_exit` maps `-9`/`-15`, leaving the actual gate-runner-cut-off bug in place.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_exit_mapping.py:test_a_signal_killed_ci_run_is_unavailable_and_never_a_queued_note

chunk_findings.detail: The added assertion still only exercises `classify_exit` in-process for positive exit codes. It never starts a gate runner, kills it before it writes a result, or runs `gate status`/review locking, so it does not reproduce B8664a1e0c6’s stale `[!] queued 11m of 15m elapsed` state or the duplicate `ddflow review` processes. A regression could keep `classify_exit(..., 129/137/143) == "failed"` while a harness-killed runner still leaves a started marker with no result and `gate status` remains queued, or while two review processes for one item can run concurrently; this test would still pass.

chunk_findings.detail: After the split, `complete()` lives in `finish.py`, so its references to `_load_fresh`, `fold`, `_dispose`, `_complete_umbrellas_above`, etc. are looked up in `finish.py`’s globals, not in the package facade. Re-exporting those names from `ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/__init__.py` makes them importable, but it does not make old monkeypatch paths effective: a test doing `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete, "_load_fresh", fake)` (or patching `fold`, or patching `complete` to intercept umbrella recursion) now changes only the facade attribute, while `finish.complete` still calls the original object in `finish.py`. In the old single module, patching `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete.fold` with a raising function would make `complete()` raise; after the split the same patch is silently ignored.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/finish.py:complete

chunk_findings.detail: The change removes a line from `tests/file_size_baseline.txt`, but the stated size/layout guard baseline is `tests/guard_baselines/file_size_baseline.txt` (the same guard-baseline tree as the renamed complexity baseline). That leaves the baseline entry for the deleted `ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py` in the guard baseline, so `tests/test_lifecycle_layout.py` still sees a stale baseline entry for a file that no longer exists and the old file is not de-baselined as intended.
chunk_findings.title: tests/file_size_baseline.txt

chunk_findings.detail: The facade makes the old names importable, but it does not preserve the old monkeypatching semantics of a single module. In the old `complete.py`, a test that replaced `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._close_bugs` (or `_dispose`, etc.) changed the global used by all calls inside that module. After this split, the package attribute is only a lazy re-export; the docstring itself says tests that replace a name must patch the defining submodule. Thus `monkeypatch.setattr("ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._close_bugs", fake)` before calling `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete.complete(...)` will bind `fake` only on the package, while the `complete` function in `finish.py` resolves `_close_bugs` from its own submodule namespace, so the real implementation still runs. This breaks the stated no-behaviour-change / monkeypatched-name guarantee.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/__init__.py (`_reexport.reexport`)

chunk_findings.detail: `abandon` imports `_dispose` directly into its own module namespace (`from .dispose import _dispose`) and then calls that module-global. Monkeypatching the old/facade helper name, e.g. `monkeypatch.setattr("ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._dispose", lambda *a: {"worktree": "fake"})` (or even `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete.dispose._dispose` after import), therefore does **not** change the helper used by `abandon`: it still calls the original `_dispose` bound in `abandoning.py`. A test that patches the old complete-module name to avoid real worktree/branch cleanup will still execute the real disposal side effects and return the real disposal dict, violating the split’s stated goal of preserving monkeypatched names.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/abandoning.py:17 (`abandon` / `_dispose`)

chunk_findings.detail: The split changes monkeypatch semantics for the old facade. `_auto_complete_unavailable` calls `_only_unavailable` and `_approved_force` as globals in `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete.approval`, and `_override_by_approval` calls `_approved_force` there. In the deleted single module, those calls resolved through `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete`, so tests or callers that monkeypatched `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._approved_force` (or `_only_unavailable`) changed the behaviour of the helpers. After this split, assigning `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._approved_force = lambda *a, **k: (True, {"approval": "fake"}, "")` only changes the facade attribute; a call to `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._auto_complete_unavailable(..., approval="", agent=<agent-marker>)` with a verdict such as `v.unmet_gates=["gate"]`, `v.coverage_gaps=["gate"]`, `v.blockers=["required gates"]`, `v.may_complete=False` still uses the original `_approved_force` in `approval.py` and can return the real refusal instead of the fake stamp. That violates the stated no-behaviour-change / monkeypatched-name compatibility.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/approval.py:_auto_complete_unavailable

chunk_findings.detail: The malformed-regression-test pre-check validates the `regression_test` argument, but the close that follows spends the `tests` argument: `_close_bugs` calls `bug_fixed(..., regression_test=tests, ...)`. Nothing in the helper ties `regression_test` to `tests`, so a malformed value in `tests` can bypass the validate-before-spend check. For example, with `tests=["tests/foo.py"]`, `regression_test="tests/test_x.py::test_ok"`, `lint_exempt=""`, `closing=True`, and `pending=["B1"]`, `_close_arg_refusal` returns `None` because `regression_test` is a valid node id, then `_close_bugs` passes the file path to `bug_fixed`, which refuses only after the operator’s single override has been spent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/closing.py:_close_arg_refusal

chunk_findings.detail: The split changes the module where `complete`'s callable globals live. `finish.py` binds every helper and even the top-level `complete` into its own module namespace at import time (`from ..._base import _load_fresh`, `from .checks import ...`, and the recursive call `done = complete(...)` at line 259). Existing monkeypatches that target the old public path `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._load_fresh` (or `...complete.complete`) now only change the facade package attribute; `finish.complete` still calls the original objects. For example, `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete, "_load_fresh", fake)` before calling `complete(repo, item)` makes `fake` visible via the package `dir()` but line 81 still calls the real `_load_fresh`, so the test hits the real repository/log instead of the fake. Likewise, a patch of `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete.complete` no longer intercepts the umbrella recursion at line 259. This is a behavior change from the old single module and defeats the facade's monkeypatched-name contract.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/finish.py:20-29, 259

chunk_findings.detail: `queue_ops` captures `_dispose` as a module-level name with `from .dispose import _dispose`. In the old single-module layout, `remove` resolved `_dispose` through `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete` at call time, so tests or callers that monkeypatched `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._dispose` changed `remove`’s behaviour. After this split, patching the facade attribute only changes the package namespace; `queue_ops.remove` still calls the function object bound in `queue_ops`. For example, `monkeypatch.setattr("ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._dispose", fake)` followed by `remove(repo, "x")` still executes the real `_dispose`, so any test that suppresses/records disposal through the old monkeypatch target fails or production patching silently does nothing. This is a behaviour change relative to the stated “monkeypatched name” compatibility goal.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/queue_ops.py:15

chunk_findings.detail: The SZ-ratchet baseline line for the deleted `ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py` is removed from the wrong path. The change’s stated baseline location is `tests/guard_baselines/file_size_baseline.txt` (and the sibling guard baselines live under `tests/guard_baselines/…`), but this diff only edits `tests/file_size_baseline.txt`; the manifest contains no edit to the guard-baseline copy. If the SZ-ratchet reads the guard-baseline copy, it still contains `ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py | 30393 | …`, so after the source file is deleted the ratchet still sees a stale baselined path and the split does not actually clear the SZ-ratchet failure.
chunk_findings.title: tests/file_size_baseline.txt

chunk_findings.detail: The test only proves that the facade attribute and the defining submodule attribute are the same object; it does not preserve the old monkeypatching contract. After the split, a helper such as `_failed_review` is defined in `checks.py` and used by the implementation in `finish.py`. If an existing test does `monkeypatch.setattr("ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._failed_review", lambda *a: False)`, the new test still passes because the unpatched objects are identical, but the patch changes only the package attribute and not the global actually referenced by `finish.complete`. Thus old-path monkeypatches silently stop affecting behavior, contradicting the stated “monkeypatched name”/no-behaviour-change intent.

data.body: Open bugs jumped 50 to 110 after dx-autofile-defects went live across ~5 self-assessing phases, and the filing dedup check is token/keyword-based only, so semantic near-duplicates of one root cause are filed under different titles (proven this session: B0419c114ef + B16f7e5be1a + B-review-delta-failed-needs-reason were one bug). There is no global sweep: dedupe runs only as a per-item merge gate. Add  (and strengthen  for bugs): scan the OPEN bug list for near-duplicates (symptom/root-cause semantic matching, not just token overlap), report the clusters, and  the younger ones onto a canonical member (never auto-close without the operator's spot-check on groups). Reuse in  so future auto-filing is semantically deduped too. r-reuse-core, r-small-files. Tests: two bugs with paraphrased descriptions of the same cause get clustered; two genuinely distinct causes do not.
